deep_why: The paper tackles expert disagreement in medical image annotation. The core problem is that when multiple pathologists label the same image, they often disagree, yet most datasets hide this by forcing a single ground truth. CytoCrowd provides both raw disagreement and a gold standard by asking: what properties let us measure if an annotation algorithm successfully resolves conflicting expert opinions? The soundness comes from separating measurement concerns—use the gold standard to evaluate pure accuracy on clean data, then separately test how well algorithms predict what the next expert would say from the messy four-way disagreement. This works because disagreement itself has structure: if four experts split, the splits reveal something about ambiguous cases rather than error. By keeping both views, you can train models on clean data while validating they gracefully handle real-world uncertainty.

Search and retrieval for language models faces a timing problem: as new documents arrive constantly, yesterday's search index becomes less useful without expensive retraining. FlowRAG asks: which small part of a retriever should change to adapt to new documents without forgetting old knowledge? The method works because it adds learnable prompts at each layer of the encoder, allowing each layer to shift its semantic interpretation slightly based on new data. The generator-guided loss then aligns these decisions with what the downstream language model will actually reward—fixing a retrieval choice is only good if downstream generation improves. This is sound because you are not retraining everything equally; you target the parts that can adapt most cheaply while locking the core knowledge, mimicking how humans update beliefs about a slowly evolving world without unlearning everything.

The talk argues data is consumable rather than infinitely reusable, grounded in privacy mathematics. The core principle is that any meaningful public release of data about real people necessarily leaks some information about those individuals, and these leaks accumulate each time the dataset is shared or queried. This is sound because information is additive: if analysis A reveals something about person X, and analysis B reveals something about person X, an observer seeing both results learns more than from either alone. The legal concept of mosaic effect reinforces this—seemingly harmless facts combine into intimate portraits. This matters because it means data use itself has limits: if ten analyses each leak 0.01 of privacy, the total loss is real. Treating data use as a rival good implies governance systems where access is budgeted and monitored.

Training on graphs while protecting individual users requires bounding how much any single user's data can affect the learning outcome. SaGD addresses the hardness of computing this bound: in a graph, removing one node affects its neighbors' training signals via message passing, and those neighbors' changes propagate further, creating nested dependencies. The method works by reweighting edges rather than pruning them, allowing a tight mathematical bound on maximum influence without losing graph structure. This is sound because you can prove an upper limit on how far influence spreads using analysis of the propagation scheme: if you control edge weights carefully, you can prove that any user's removal changes the final model by at most a known amount. This allows adding privacy noise that is proportionally correct rather than conservative, since you're not overestimating the hidden dependencies.

When humans and language models co-produce knowledge (like on Wikipedia or GitHub), the system has feedback loops: if the model learns from human-written content, then produces content that humans later learn from, the quality of human contributions can decay. The paper builds a dynamical model tracking archive quality, human skill, model skill, and content volume over time. It works because these quantities are governed by flow equations: human contribution rate depends on perceived value of archived knowledge, model contribution rate depends on its training data, and both learning pathways produce measurable skill changes. By simulating these flows under different policies, the method reveals regime shifts—the boundary where archive quality starts degrading despite more content. This is sound because it captures the core feedback: poor training data produces poor model outputs, which then become new poor training data, compounding decay over time.

Clustering bipartite graphs to find dense cliques is hard because you must avoid expensive enumeration of all possible cliques. ECRC uses a counting insight: instead of listing cliques, count how many cliques contain each edge, then weight edges by this count. Edges that participate in many dense cliques get high weight, enabling standard clustering to naturally find those cliques. This is sound because any true biclique—a complete subgraph between two sides—will have all its edges count equally high, making them cluster together. Edges that are not part of dense cliques count low and separate out. The approximation guarantee means: any solution this algorithm finds provably recovers all true bicliques above a size threshold. This works because counting-based weight assignment directly reflects clique membership without enumerating them.

Topic modeling at web scale must be cheap and interpretable, but embedding spaces are high-dimensional and topics blur together. PRISM trains a sentence encoder using sparse labels from a large language model, then clusters in that learned embedding space. The method works because a teacher-student setup allows you to distill expensive model reasoning into a cheap student: the large model provides high-quality labels on a small sample, revealing what good topic separation looks like; the student embedding model learns to arrange that sample well, and when applied to the full corpus, it generalizes because the geometry of the training sample reflects the true topic structure. This is sound because thresholded clustering in a learned space with teacher guidance separates inherently overlapping topics: the learned geometry amplifies differences the model deemed important.

Social movements generate emotional signals across platforms, and journalists need early warning when discourse shifts, especially around external events like elections. SMART combines data collection with a transformer-based forecasting model that predicts future emotional intensity. The method works because emotions on social media respond to external events with predictable delays: trauma discussions spike after news of injustice, then decay; the transformer learns these temporal patterns and can forecast when the next spike will occur or intensity drop. This is sound because human emotional response to events is non-random: communities process news synchronously, producing correlated posting patterns that compress into learnable dynamics. By detecting when predicted emotion diverges from actual emotion, journalists spot when discourse has shifted course—an early signal something unexpected happened.

Language models are often opaque: users cannot see why the model chose a particular response or how it reasons. IntraAI exposes internal signals—alignment patterns, staged reasoning—through interactive visualization. The method works because understanding causation in model behavior requires showing the steps: if you display how attention focused on certain phrases or how certain features activated, users can reverse-engineer the decision pathway and build intuition about when to trust the model. This is sound because human understanding requires a bridge: showing the reasoning steps makes the model's behavior predictable rather than magical, enabling users to mentally simulate what the model will do next and calibrate when to accept or override its suggestions.

Multimodal models that learn features capturing spurious correlations fail when data distribution shifts—what worked on training examples breaks in deployment. SCLF enforces robustness by explicitly selecting only causal features, using a gating mechanism to zero out features that vary across environments. The method works because true causal features remain stable across distribution shifts by definition: if a feature causally determines the label, it must be useful regardless of how the background distribution changes. By combining adversarial training (which discovers what changes under distribution shifts) with feature stability scoring (which rewards features that don't vary), the algorithm filters to a small set of truly stable signals. This is sound because this filters out spurious correlations—artifacts that correlate in one environment but break in another—retaining only features that generalize.

Academic citations are supposed to support claims, but miscitations occur when a paper cites another work that actually contradicts or fails to support the claim. Detecting this requires semantic reasoning over the citation graph. LAGMiD uses language models for deep reasoning (which can catch subtle meaning) but distills that into a scalable graph network. The method works because citation context matters: what claim does a paper make about the referenced work, and does the reference's content actually support that claim? Language models excel at this semantic matching. Distillation works because once the language model identifies miscitations, the graph neural network learns patterns—if miscitations cluster in certain network neighborhoods or citation types, structure predicts them. This is sound because it offloads expensive reasoning to the model only when needed while letting the scalable graph network handle routine cases.

Time series data from web services involves many variables (traffic, latency, errors) interacting over time, and you must estimate the time-varying dependency structure. Kronecker products offer a factorization: instead of a single large entangled network, express the dependencies as a combination of mode-specific smaller networks. The method works because real tensor time series often have structure across modes—relationships between servers may follow patterns different from relationships between time points—and factoring these reduces the space of possible networks to search. This is sound because a Kronecker product of two small networks encodes much fewer relationships than a monolithic network of combined size, making patterns visible and computation tractable. As data evolves over time, you can update each factor cheaply, enabling streaming.

Distributed fine-tuning of language models splits computation between edge devices and cloud servers to reduce edge bandwidth, but the cloud can invert intermediate embeddings to recover the user's original input, a privacy break. PrivSplit splits each embedding: the edge sends a public part to the cloud and keeps a private part locally. The method works because the private part is mathematically compensated during training: if the full embedding should go through a computation, the cloud performs its part on the public embedding, then the edge applies a correction term that restores exactly what would have happened with the full embedding. This is sound because this is lossless: the model learns identically whether the private part is hidden or visible. An attacker with only the public part cannot invert to the original input because information is provably missing, yet training proceeds without loss of accuracy.

DNS responses can be manipulated to redirect users or block domains, but detection is hard in dynamic resolution environments where a single domain may have many edge servers. The paper uses CNAME chain analysis: when a domain resolves, it may follow a chain of aliases before reaching a final IP, and this path has structure. By tracking resolution paths over many domains, anomalies emerge—if a domain's path suddenly changes or resolves to unexpected intermediaries, it indicates manipulation. This is sound because legitimate resolution chains are stable: a domain operator controls which servers serve content, and this setup doesn't change randomly. Manipulation often requires injecting false intermediaries or rerouting the chain, creating detectable deviations. Large-scale measurement reveals patterns: certain operators use similar tactics, making their fingerprints visible.

Web applications evolve constantly—layouts change, elements move, new features appear—but there's no large-scale dataset showing real patterns of this evolution. The paper archives 1,000 snapshots per website over time, recording the structural DOM hierarchy with timestamps. The dataset works because structure persists even when content changes: moving an element or adding a section creates a measurable change in XPath positions, and these changes follow patterns. Some elements move frequently, others rarely; some updates happen in bursts around deployment cycles, others gradually. With 246 million timestamped positions, researchers can model evolution as a stochastic process—predicting when the next major layout change occurs or detecting breakage patterns. This enables building tools that automatically adapt to structural changes rather than breaking.
